Pacific dogwood often has opposite leaves, whose prominent veins curve toward the tip. Its conspicuous white structures in the flowering season are bracts surrounding the cluster of much smaller flowers.

Rounded lobes and acorns, pale peeling bark with horizontal markings, and opposite leaves with curved veins. Each set of features leads in a different direction. A regional key can then help identify the species more precisely. It is a rather agreeable exercise in noticing details that might otherwise escape one's attention.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: oak, birch and dogwood

tracks.announcement_text:
A tree contains two quite different systems for transporting materials. Xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals, chiefly from the roots toward the leaves. Phloem carries sugars and other materials from places where they are supplied to places where they are needed or stored.

Between the two systems in many woody stems lies a layer of growing tissue called the vascular cambium. It produces new xylem toward the inside and new phloem toward the outside. Much of the wood in a trunk consists of accumulated secondary xylem.

The bark is not merely a jacket of dead material. Its outer portions protect the stem, but living phloem and other living tissues may lie within it. The transport system is distributed through a tree's roots, trunk, branches and leaves.

I find it quite remarkable that what appears to be a solid, motionless trunk belongs to such an active arrangement of living tissues and transport pathways.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: a tree's living plumbing

tracks.announcement_text:
In many temperate trees, wood produced during one growing season differs from wood produced later in that season. The resulting contrast can form a visible annual ring. A cross-section of the trunk may therefore contain a long record of growth.

A wide ring does not tell us simply that the year was warm. Water availability, temperature, injury, competition and the tree's own circumstances can all influence growth. Some trees form unusual or incomplete rings. Researchers compare patterns from multiple specimens to establish dates more reliably, a practice known as crossdating in dendrochronology.

The trunk grows thicker because new wood is produced near its outer living tissues. It does not enlarge by stretching each of the old rings outward.

A series of rings can be a remarkable record, but reading that record requires a little more than counting lines. The interesting part is discovering which of their variations can be interpreted with confidence.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: rings and seasons

tracks.announcement_text:
A tree and a mushroom may grow very close to each other, but they belong to different kingdoms of life. Green plants generally manufacture sugars using light through photosynthesis. Fungi do not photosynthesize. They obtain organic nutrients from their surroundings or from other organisms.

Their cells also differ. Fungal cell walls commonly contain chitin and glucans, whereas plant cell walls are chiefly built around cellulose. In the evolutionary tree of life, fungi share a more recent common ancestor with animals than with plants.

This does not make a mushroom a sort of animal, any more than the absence of green leaves makes it a plant without leaves. Fungi have their own diverse forms and ways of living. Some help plants obtain nutrients, some decompose dead wood, and some cause disease.

The mushroom beside a tree may therefore belong to an entirely different organism, with a quite different method of obtaining the materials it needs to grow.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: fungi are not plants

tracks.announcement_text:
Consider a mushroom growing from a fallen log. The part that catches your attention may have appeared quite recently, but the fungus producing it can have been growing inside the wood for a considerable time.

Many fungi consist of slender filaments called hyphae. A collection of those filaments forms a mycelium, which may extend through soil, wood or other material. The visible mushroom is a reproductive structure, often produced by a much less conspicuous fungal body.

A mushroom is therefore not quite analogous to a whole tree. It is more helpful to think of it as one structure produced by the larger organism. That analogy is not exact, either; the life histories of plants and fungi differ in important ways.

Not every fungus forms a mycelium or a recognizable mushroom. Yeasts provide familiar examples of fungi that commonly grow as individual cells. It is an extraordinarily varied kingdom.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: the mushroom and the mycelium

tracks.announcement_text:
A seed contains a young plant embryo, usually accompanied by protective tissues and some provision for early growth. A fungal spore is a different sort of reproductive or dispersal unit. It may be a single cell or have several cells, depending on the fungus.

The spores of many mushrooms form on the gills, in tubes, or on other spore-producing surfaces. Under suitable circumstances a spore may germinate and begin growing into fungal filaments. Fungi can produce spores through sexual or asexual reproduction, and their life cycles vary considerably.

It is tempting to call a spore a very small seed, because both can contribute to the spread of an organism. But that comparison conceals the differences in structure and development. A mushroom does not scatter little embryonic trees, and a tree seed is more than a spore with a rather elaborate coat.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: spores and seeds

tracks.announcement_text:
Many fungi obtain nutrients in a particularly interesting manner. Instead of swallowing a piece of wood or leaf, the fungus secretes enzymes into the material around it. These help break larger molecules into smaller ones that the fungal cells can absorb.

A fungus feeding on dead organic material is called a saprotroph. Other fungi obtain resources from living hosts and may harm them. Still others enter mutually beneficial associations, such as the partnerships that form between many fungi and plant roots.

The fact that a mushroom is growing beside a tree does not tell you immediately which relationship it has with that tree. It may be connected to the roots, decomposing a buried piece of wood, or growing from something else entirely.

I find this way of feeding particularly elegant. The fungus can extend its hyphae through a material and carry out much of the necessary digestion outside its own cells.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: how a fungus eats

tracks.announcement_text:
One of the most useful observations when describing a mushroom is the shape of its underside. Some have gills, thin plates that extend from near the stalk toward the edge of the cap. Others have little openings called pores, which lead into tubes. Still others have blunt folds, or downward-pointing spines resembling teeth.

These structures provide surfaces associated with the formation of spores. Their appearance helps mycologists sort the tremendous variety of mushrooms into recognizable forms. A gilled mushroom and a mushroom with a spongy underside may suggest quite different possibilities for identification.

Look also at where the mushroom grows, the shape of its stalk, and the other features that a regional guide describes. The underside alone is not sufficient for a species identification, much less a judgment about whether a fungus can be eaten.

Gills, pores, folds or teeth. Four useful words for describing something you might find in a forest.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: gills, pores, folds and teeth

tracks.announcement_text:
A mushroom with a cap and a stalk may look rather conventional from above. Look underneath, however, and you might find a surface resembling a fine sponge instead of the familiar radiating gills. The little pores lead into tubes. This is a characteristic form among boletes.

Boletes are a diverse collection of fungi, and many form associations with the roots of trees. The color of the pore surface, the markings on the stalk, the cap and the habitat can all be informative when distinguishing them. Some species change color when injured, but that response is not a universal identification test.

There are toxic boletes, and the presence of pores is certainly not a guarantee of edibility. For the moment, a useful observation is simply that the spore-bearing surface has tubes rather than blades. It is a very different arrangement from the gills of a typical agaric mushroom.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: boletes

tracks.announcement_text:
The Pacific golden chanterelle is one of the regional fungi whose underside is particularly interesting. Rather than having thin, knife-like gills, it often has blunt ridges that fork and extend partway down the stalk. The whole surface has a more folded appearance.

Other mushrooms can share the yellow or orange colors of chanterelles while having true blade-like gills. The color of a cap is therefore a considerably weaker clue than several morphological characteristics considered together.

This is an illustration of how mycologists describe fungal structures, not an instruction for selecting wild food. A reliable species identification requires a fuller comparison, and eating a wild mushroom on the strength of an audio description would be a very poor experiment indeed.

I would remember the branching, blunt folds as a useful feature to recognize. There is a satisfying distinction between a surface that looks rather like folds in cloth and one composed of individual, delicate plates.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: the Pacific golden chanterelle

tracks.announcement_text:
Turkey-tail is a familiar fungus that can form thin, overlapping shelves on dead wood. The upper surface often displays bands of different colors arranged in arcs, rather like the markings on a spread tail.

But several fungi produce similarly colored shelves. A useful comparison lies underneath them. Turkey-tail, Trametes versicolor, has a surface with very small pores. Some similar-looking species in the genus Stereum have an underside that is smooth rather than porous.

The difference is useful even when the upper surfaces look almost identical. A photograph showing only the colorful bands may conceal the feature that would help most with the identification.

There is quite a lovely variety of shelf fungi in the forest. Examine the surface and the material on which each grows. It is best to regard any provisional name as a hypothesis until the relevant distinguishing features have been checked.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: turkey-tail and its lookalikes

tracks.announcement_text:
Not every mushroom has a surface made of gills or pores. Some fungi form spines, from which spores are released. A particularly elegant example in the Pacific Northwest is the bear's-head fungus, Hericium abietis.

Its fruiting structure can form pale, branching masses with long, hanging teeth. It often grows on conifer wood. Compare that branching form with the more compact, relatively unbranched appearance commonly associated with lion's mane, another member of the same genus.

Species of Hericium can be rather similar, and the appearance of a fruiting body changes as it develops. The host wood, branching structure and finer characteristics may all be needed for a confident name. The white color and hanging teeth alone do not establish a species or its suitability as food.

What a curious little architecture. A fungus can grow something resembling a cluster of icicles and use that structure to produce its spores.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: the bear's-head fungus

tracks.announcement_text:
The morels belong to a genus called Morchella, and there is more than one species. Their familiar pitted caps can resemble a little honeycomb, with ridges surrounding numerous depressions.

Other fungi have wrinkled, folded, or otherwise irregular caps and are commonly grouped under the name false morels. That common label does not describe a single species or even a single genus. A general resemblance to a morel can hide quite important differences.

Some of these lookalikes are dangerous if consumed. Even true morels have caused illness, particularly when eaten raw or undercooked. I would not advise anyone to identify mushrooms for eating from a short spoken description. Species boundaries and identification require considerably more evidence than a resemblance in cap shape.

For our study, the distinction is morphological: pits surrounded by ridges, as opposed to other arrangements of folds and wrinkles. Notice those structures, and consult an expert reference rather than letting the familiar shape settle the matter.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: morels and false morels

tracks.announcement_text:
A cap and stalk are only two of the many shapes a fungus can produce. Coral fungi may have upright branching structures, and club fungi may have slender columns. Cup fungi can form a little bowl whose surface bears spores. Jelly fungi may have soft, gelatinous fruiting structures. Puffballs produce spores internally, which can be released as the structure matures.

These names describe appearances, not necessarily a close evolutionary relationship. Two distant fungal groups can produce somewhat similar shapes, just as unrelated plants can independently acquire similar leaves.

A morphological description is valuable because it gives another observer something to compare. Say that the structure is branching, cup-shaped, or gelatinous, and record what it grows upon. That is often more useful than guessing a species at once. There is an extraordinary amount of fungal architecture to discover beyond the familiar umbrella-shaped mushroom.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: fungi in unfamiliar shapes

tracks.announcement_text:
The familiar image of a red mushroom with pale spots is often inspired by fly agaric, a member of the genus Amanita. Another member, the death cap, can look much less conspicuous. Both illustrate why an attractive or familiar appearance tells us remarkably little about a mushroom's toxicity.

The genus contains species with very different properties, including some that can cause fatal poisoning. The remains of a veil, the base of the stalk, the gills, and other features can assist an experienced mycologist. Yet these features can change with age or be obscured, and a cap's color may vary.

There is a great deal to learn about Amanita as a collection of living organisms. It is not necessary to turn that study into an experiment in eating them. If an identification matters for safety, a qualified local expert is essential. An appealing photograph or an apparently simple rule will not suffice.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: the genus Amanita

tracks.announcement_text:
Wood contains cellulose and other carbohydrates within a complex structure that includes lignin. Different wood-decaying fungi have different abilities to break down those materials.

White-rot fungi can degrade lignin as well as carbohydrates, and the decayed wood may become pale and fibrous. Brown-rot fungi predominantly remove the carbohydrates while leaving a modified, lignin-rich residue. The wood may become brown, brittle and cracked into little blocks.

Neither form of decay is merely a matter of the wood becoming wet. Fungal enzymes and related chemical processes alter the material itself. Over time, these processes help release nutrients and return carbon to the wider ecosystem.

The texture of a decaying log can therefore provide clues about what has been happening within it. I would not infer a precise species from that texture, but a pale fibrous fragment and a dark cubically cracked fragment can suggest two very different forms of fungal activity.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: the fungi that recycle wood

tracks.announcement_text:
Fungi in the genus Armillaria can live in wood and, in some circumstances, cause serious root disease in trees. Their presence may not be obvious from the leaves alone. Beneath bark, some form pale fungal growth, and dark cord-like structures called rhizomorphs may extend through soil or wood.

The mushrooms associated with these fungi may appear in groups near a tree or from buried wood. Yet mushrooms beside a tree are not, by themselves, proof that the living tree is infected or likely to fall. The material from which the fungus is growing may already be dead.

Diagnosing root disease requires careful examination of the tree, its roots and its surroundings. A qualified arborist can assess a potentially hazardous tree. For our purposes, Armillaria illustrates the difference between a visible fruiting structure and an organism whose activity may extend well beyond that structure.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: Armillaria and tree roots

tracks.announcement_text:
Many plants have fungal partners associated with their roots. These associations are called mycorrhizae. The plant can supply organic carbon derived from photosynthesis, while the fungus can extend its fine hyphae into the surrounding soil and help the plant acquire nutrients such as phosphorus or nitrogen.

There are different forms of this association. Ectomycorrhizal fungi may form a sheath around fine root tips and grow between root cells. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi form intricately branched structures inside root cells, although the plant's cell membrane remains between the fungal structure and the cell's contents.

The exchanges depend on the organisms and their conditions. They need not benefit every partner equally at every moment. It is an especially interesting way of studying the relations between trees, other plants and fungi, because an organism's abilities can be extended through association with a different organism.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: mycorrhizae

tracks.announcement_text:
The expression wood-wide web refers to the possibility of plants being connected through shared mycorrhizal fungi. Such connections do occur. There are also extraordinary plants that obtain some or all of their organic carbon through fungal associations rather than ordinary green photosynthesis.

But a shared connection does not settle every question about what moves through it. Researchers must distinguish the transfer of a substance from its consequences for the growth of the organisms involved, and establish which route the transfer actually followed.

There has been considerable scientific debate over claims that forest trees routinely favor their offspring or deliberately send resources to needy neighbors through fungal networks. The evidence does not justify treating such stories as a universal account of forest behavior.

The genuine partnerships are already fascinating. I would rather preserve the distinction between a demonstrated connection, a measured exchange, and an attractive interpretation of what that exchange means.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: the wood-wide web

tracks.announcement_text:
A lichen may form a crust on a stone, a little leafy patch on bark, or a branching structure that hangs from a tree. Yet a lichen is not simply a plant growing upon that surface.

It is an association centered on a fungus and one or more photosynthetic partners, often green algae or cyanobacteria. The fungus contributes much of the structure, while its photosynthetic partners can supply organic carbon. Other organisms can also be part of these associations, which are more complex than the simplest two-part description suggests.

Mosses, by contrast, are plants. They have tiny leaf-like structures and a different organization, even when they grow beside lichens on the same trunk.

I find lichens rather delightful because of the variety of forms these associations produce. A crust, a leafy lobe, and a little branching tuft may all invite investigation as lichens, although further characteristics are needed to name them.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: lichens

tracks.announcement_text:
If I were recording an unfamiliar mushroom for a research collection, I would begin with what can be observed without assigning it a name. What is the cap's shape? Does the underside have gills, pores, folds or spines? What does the stalk look like, including its base? Is the fungus growing on soil, a log, or some other material?

A useful record includes the date, the location, nearby trees, and photographs from several angles. Changes with age can be important. Some species can only be distinguished confidently using microscopic characters or genetic evidence.

An uncertain identification is a perfectly respectable observation. Never use a short description, an app, or a photograph alone to decide that a wild mushroom is safe to eat. If you suspect someone has eaten a poisonous or unidentified wild mushroom, contact your local poison center or emergency medical service immediately. Do not wait for symptoms or for the fungus to receive a name.

For my notebook, a careful description is worth considerably more than an impressive but unsupported Latin name.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: observing a mushroom

tracks.announcement_text:
A good research question is not necessarily an elaborate one. Suppose two plants of the same species grow to different heights. There are several possible reasons. Perhaps one received more light, perhaps its soil was different, or perhaps the plants already differed when the observations began.

A hypothesis is a proposed explanation that can be investigated. It should lead to expectations that can be compared with observations. If a proposed explanation predicts one result and the observations consistently show another, the explanation may need revision.

Not all sciences can arrange their subjects in a laboratory. Astronomers cannot repeat the formation of a particular star, but they can compare observations and predictions made by different accounts of stellar development.

The ability to distinguish a possible explanation from the evidence for it is one of the most useful habits in research. It makes a little room for the discovery of something one had not anticipated.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: a question in the laboratory

tracks.announcement_text:
Imagine that we wish to investigate whether the amount of light affects plant growth. Giving one plant more light but also changing its soil, water and temperature would make the result difficult to interpret. Which of those differences was responsible?

In a controlled comparison, we try to keep other relevant conditions similar while deliberately varying the factor of interest. Replication gives us more than one observation in each condition, so an unusual individual does not determine the entire conclusion. Random assignment, when suitable, can help reduce the influence of preexisting differences.

Controls do not guarantee that every alternative explanation has been removed. There may be something we did not think to measure. That is one reason researchers describe their methods and uncertainties rather than simply reporting an attractive result.

The point of a fair comparison is to make the evidence more informative, not to arrange for a hypothesis to be correct.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: a fair comparison

tracks.announcement_text:
In one useful account of acid and base chemistry, an acid can donate a proton, while a base can accept one. A proton here is a hydrogen nucleus. This is the Brønsted–Lowry description, and it helps explain many reactions involving acids and bases.

The pH scale describes the activity of hydrogen ions on a logarithmic scale. In comparable conditions, a decrease of one pH unit corresponds to a tenfold increase in hydrogen-ion activity. A difference of two units is therefore a hundredfold difference, not merely twice as much.

Acid strength describes how readily an acid donates a proton in a given setting. Concentration describes how much of a substance is present in a given amount of solution. These are different properties.

There is quite a lot of chemistry concealed within that little number on a laboratory instrument. It is especially important not to confuse a low pH with a complete description of the solution's composition or hazards.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: acids, bases and pH

tracks.announcement_text:
A telescope need not resolve the surface of a planet to discover that the planet may be there. When an orbiting planet passes between its star and our line of sight, it blocks a little of the star's light. This event is called a transit.

Astronomers can record the star's brightness over time and look for a repeating dip. The interval between successive transits helps establish the planet's orbital period. The depth of a transit can help estimate the planet's size relative to the star, with suitable models of the geometry and the star's brightness.

Other events, such as eclipses between stars, can also produce dips. Further observations are needed to establish that a planetary explanation is the appropriate one.

I find it rather delightful that something as small as a slight reduction in light can provide information about an otherwise unresolved world. In this case, the shadow is a measurement.
tracks.title: astra's observatory: finding planets by shadows

tracks.announcement_text:
Suppose I were to receive a little book from my future self. I read it, keep it carefully, and one day take that very book into the past to give it to my younger self. The contents remain the same throughout this curious arrangement.

I can explain how I acquired the book: my older self brought it to me. And I can explain how my older self acquired it: someone brought it to me when I was younger. But if nobody else ever writes it, where did the information in the book originate?

This is the bootstrap paradox, an example of a causal loop. Each event has a cause elsewhere in the loop, but there is no source of the information outside it. That is a peculiar problem about origins, not necessarily a logical contradiction. A consistent loop may be mathematically conceivable even if we have no demonstrated means of traveling into the past.

The book's physical survival would raise further questions, of course. But even if we considered only its words, the original question would remain. Who is the author, friend? How curious.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the bootstrap paradox

tracks.announcement_text:
Imagine a machine that could carry a traveler into the past, and a unique ticket that must remain intact for that particular departure to take place. The traveler departs with the ticket, arrives before the departure, and destroys the ticket before it can be used.

If the ticket is destroyed, the traveler cannot leave. But if the traveler never leaves, who destroys the ticket? This is a version of the grandfather paradox. Its difficulty is not merely that information has no obvious origin. The proposed event removes a condition necessary for that very event to happen.

There are various hypothetical responses. Perhaps the history must remain self-consistent, and the proposed destruction cannot occur in that history. Perhaps an imagined model allows alternative histories, though that would require a different account of what traveling into the past means.

None of these possibilities establishes that such a machine exists. They illustrate the difference between describing a time-travel adventure and constructing a coherent account of its causality. I find the ticket a rather useful little object for keeping that distinction in view.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the grandfather paradox

tracks.announcement_text:
A path through spacetime represents a succession of events. In relativity, a timelike path is one that could locally be followed by a massive object moving more slowly than light. Ordinarily we picture such a path progressing without returning to an earlier event in its own history.

Certain mathematical solutions of general relativity permit a rather unusual arrangement. A timelike path can form a closed curve, returning to the very spacetime event from which it began. Locally, the traveler could still move forward according to their own clock. It is the larger geometry of the path that makes the loop possible in the model.

This is called a closed timelike curve. It is not a demonstrated transport system. Whether physically realistic conditions could produce such a geometry, and whether other principles of physics would prevent it, are separate questions.

A solution to a set of equations is a mathematical achievement. Establishing that nature can realize that solution requires considerably more. Those two accomplishments deserve their own places in our little pocket dimension.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · closed timelike curves

tracks.announcement_text:
Imagine a photograph of a pony beside a tree. It records something about where both were at a particular moment. Now imagine a succession of photographs, extending from earlier moments to later ones, each with its own time as well as its spatial position.

In relativity, a worldline is the path of an idealized pointlike object through spacetime. An object standing still in a room still has a worldline, because it continues to exist through successive moments. An extended object occupies a more elaborate region of spacetime than a single line.

There are three spatial coordinates and a temporal coordinate in ordinary relativistic spacetime. Time has a different role in the geometry from the spatial directions; it is not simply another direction in a room along which one can ordinarily wander.

I enjoy considering a history as a figure rather than a succession of isolated pictures. The worldline gives that intuition a precise mathematical form. It is a description of the object's history, rather than an additional physical thread trailing behind it.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · a worldline

tracks.announcement_text:
Suppose two flashes occur at distant positions. Observers wish to determine whether the flashes occurred at the same time. They must account for the time taken by light to travel from the flashes to their instruments, and they need a way of synchronizing clocks at different places.

Special relativity tells us that even after making those corrections consistently, observers in relative motion may disagree about the simultaneity of sufficiently separated events. Each has an inertial reference frame, with its own consistent way of assigning spatial positions and times.

This is not merely an optical illusion caused by someone standing closer to one of the flashes. The Lorentz transformations, which relate measurements in the two frames, mix spatial position and time. Events simultaneous in one frame need not be simultaneous in another.

For events that can causally influence one another, the ordering is preserved. That distinction matters. Relativity changes the notion of a universal distant present without allowing a cause to be arbitrarily placed after its effect.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the relativity of simultaneity

tracks.announcement_text:
Suppose a spacecraft passes Earth at eight tenths of the speed of light, maintaining a steady velocity during a particular portion of its voyage. Its traveler measures one year passing on the onboard clock. In the simplified Earth reference frame, the interval between the same two events is about one year and eight months.

The difference is called time dilation. The traveler's own clock works quite normally from the traveler's perspective. Their thoughts, breathing, and other physical processes do not seem to be moving in slow motion to them. The difference arises when the elapsed time is compared between reference frames.

At ordinary everyday velocities, the effect is exceedingly small. At velocities approaching that of light, the difference becomes quite substantial. Relativistic time differences have been measured using particles and precise clocks.

There is a lovely distinction here, friend. Time dilation does not mean that one's clock has developed a mechanical fault. It means that the geometry of spacetime gives different relations between intervals of time and space in different frames.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · time dilation

tracks.announcement_text:
Two twins begin together. One remains on Earth, while the other makes a very fast journey to a distant place, turns around, and comes home. When they meet again, the traveler may have experienced less elapsed time than the twin who stayed behind.

But special relativity allows each inertial observer to describe a moving clock as ticking more slowly. Why, then, do the two twins not each conclude that the other must be younger when they meet?

Their complete journeys are different. The traveling twin changes direction and changes inertial reference frames. The two paths through spacetime begin and end at the same events, yet they need not have the same elapsed proper time. Proper time is what a clock following its own path measures.

Acceleration is important in explaining why the simple symmetry argument fails, but the result can be calculated from the entire paths, not just the brief turnaround. Upon reunion they can compare their clocks directly. The so-called paradox is a useful lesson in comparing complete histories rather than isolated portions of them.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the twin paradox

tracks.announcement_text:
Consider two very precise clocks, one slightly higher than the other in Earth's gravitational field. General relativity predicts that the lower clock will tick a little more slowly, relative to the higher one, when the other relevant effects have been accounted for.

The difference is extremely small for the height of an ordinary room. Nevertheless, in twenty twenty-two, researchers at JILA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology reported a measurement of gravitational time dilation across a distance on the scale of a millimeter, using an extremely precise arrangement of atoms.

I find the scale of that experiment rather delightful. The difference in gravitational potential across such a short height is tiny, but the precision of the frequency measurements made the predicted difference observable. Even when the strength of gravity is nearly the same at both heights, their gravitational potential can differ.

This is not an effect reserved for black holes and adventurous stories. Clock rates depend upon gravitational conditions even here on Earth. Precision navigation systems also have to account for relativistic effects. A clock can be perfectly good and still measure a different amount of elapsed time from another perfectly good clock following a different history.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · gravity changes the rate of clocks

tracks.announcement_text:
Imagine a long spacecraft moving rapidly past an observer. Someone aboard measures the distance from its front to its back in the spacecraft's rest frame. The observer outside wishes to measure its length while it is moving.

The outside observer must determine where the front and back are at the same time, according to clocks synchronized in that observer's own frame. Special relativity predicts a shorter length along the direction of relative motion than the length measured in the spacecraft's rest frame.

This is length contraction. It is closely related to the relativity of simultaneity, because measuring the positions of both ends at the same time is an essential part of defining the length of a moving object.

The spacecraft has not been crushed by a mysterious physical pressure. In its own frame, its length is unchanged. Nor is the measured contraction simply the way the spacecraft would look in a photograph, where light from different parts may arrive at different times. The measurement and the visual appearance are different questions.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · length contraction

tracks.announcement_text:
The speed of light in a vacuum is a particularly important quantity in relativity. All inertial observers measuring it locally obtain the same value, regardless of their own steady motion relative to the source.

As a massive object is accelerated toward that speed, increasing its speed by a further amount requires progressively more energy. The energy needed to bring a massive object to exactly the speed of light would be unbounded in special relativity. Light itself travels at that speed in vacuum, without being a massive object accelerated up to it.

This does not mean that every number describing how fast two distant things separate must be smaller than the speed of light. In cosmology, distances defined across an expanding universe have a different significance from a local measurement of a passing spacecraft.

The important restriction for our purposes is local: ordinary massive objects and usable causal signals do not outrun light in vacuum. A mathematical description of a distant recession rate does not provide a little loophole through which to send a message into the past.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the cosmic speed limit

tracks.announcement_text:
Einstein's familiar equation says that the rest energy of an object equals its mass multiplied by the square of the speed of light. That speed is a very large number, and its square is larger still. A small difference in mass can therefore correspond to a considerable difference in energy.

Consider a bound physical system. The mass of the complete system depends upon its total energy, including the energy associated with its internal structure. When a nuclear reaction releases energy, the rest masses of the final material can differ from the combined rest masses of the initial material.

The equation does not say that conservation laws have ceased to apply. Energy carried away by radiation or moving particles must be included in the accounting, along with momentum. Nor is rest energy an amount one can simply extract in its entirety from an ordinary object by choosing to do so.

What I find elegant is the connection itself. Mass and energy, which might seem like entirely separate items in a description of nature, have a precise relationship in relativity.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · mass and energy

tracks.announcement_text:
Imagine a sealed container divided into two halves, with gas on one side and an empty space on the other. Remove the partition, and the gas spreads throughout the available volume. It is extraordinarily unlikely that all the molecules will soon gather back into the original half by chance.

There are far more microscopic arrangements in which the molecules are spread throughout the container than arrangements in which they are all confined to one small region. Statistical mechanics connects that multiplicity of microscopic arrangements with a quantity called entropy.

Entropy is often described as disorder. That can be a useful first image, but it is rather imprecise. A more helpful account considers how many microscopic states are consistent with the properties of the system that we observe on a larger scale. Entropy changes can also be calculated thermodynamically, using heat exchanged along a reversible path and the temperature at which that exchange occurs.

The gas has not forgotten how to move back. Its individual molecules continue to move according to physical laws. It is the extraordinary difference in the statistical weight of the possible arrangements that makes its ordinary macroscopic behavior so predictable.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · entropy

tracks.announcement_text:
A little ink disperses through a glass of water. A recording of the process played backward would show the dispersed color gathering into a small drop. We immediately recognize that the reversed recording depicts something most unlikely in ordinary circumstances.

The second law of thermodynamics says that the entropy of an isolated macroscopic system tends not to decrease. Many microscopic physical laws, on the other hoof, are reversible or approximately reversible in the relevant circumstances. How does an everyday distinction between past and future emerge from such laws?

Statistical mechanics supplies an important part of the account. Starting from a relatively special low-entropy arrangement, there are vastly more accessible microscopic arrangements corresponding to higher entropy. The usual macroscopic evolution reflects those probabilities.

There remains a deeper question about the low-entropy conditions of the early universe and the origins of the thermodynamic arrow of time. I would not wish to conceal that question by saying simply that time is disorder. Entropy helps explain why many changes have a preferred direction; it is not a complete explanation of every aspect of time.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the arrow of time

tracks.announcement_text:
Consider heat passing from a warm object to a cooler one. In ordinary circumstances the transfer proceeds toward thermal equilibrium. One does not expect the cooler object to spontaneously return the same amount of heat to the warmer object, leaving both precisely as they began.

In thermodynamics, a reversible process is an ideal limiting process that can be reversed without leaving a net change in the system and its surroundings. Heat transfer across a finite temperature difference is an example of an irreversible process: it produces entropy.

A refrigerator can transfer heat from a cooler region to a warmer one, but it requires work. We must include the refrigerator and its energy supply in the account. It has not overturned the second law.

There is a useful distinction between restoring one visible property and restoring the entire physical arrangement. You may return an object to its original temperature without returning everything around it to its original state. That is why reversibility is a more demanding idea than simply making something look as it did before.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · reversible and irreversible changes

tracks.announcement_text:
Imagine light shining upon a suitable metal surface. Under certain conditions, electrons are emitted from it. One might expect that making any light sufficiently bright would eventually supply individual electrons with enough energy to escape.

The photoelectric effect revealed a more interesting pattern. For ordinary single-photon emission, there is a threshold frequency below which the individual light quanta do not have enough energy to release an electron. The energy of a photon is proportional to the frequency of the light. Above the threshold, increasing the frequency can increase the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons.

Increasing the brightness at a fixed suitable frequency generally increases the number of photons available, and hence can increase the emission rate. It does not provide each individual photon with more energy.

This was important evidence for the quantum description of light. A bright red beam and a dim ultraviolet beam differ not merely in how much light they deliver, but in the energy associated with each photon. That is a rather remarkable distinction concealed in the color of light.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · photons and the photoelectric effect

tracks.announcement_text:
A wave spreading across water can pass through two openings and produce a pattern of reinforcement and cancellation. A collection of ordinary little balls, by contrast, would arrive as separate objects. Quantum experiments reveal features that do not fit neatly into either of these familiar pictures alone.

Light and matter can produce interference patterns, and their interactions with detectors can occur in discrete localized events. Even when particles are sent through an appropriate apparatus one at a time, their accumulated detections can reveal a pattern associated with interference.

The expression wave–particle duality draws attention to these two aspects of quantum behavior. It does not mean that an electron is an ordinary water wave on Mondays and a tiny classical ball on Tuesdays. The underlying quantum description has its own mathematical structure.

I find the distinction quite important. Familiar images can help us approach a difficult subject, but we need not insist that nature choose one of those images as its literal identity. Sometimes the new mathematical description is precisely what the old images were missing.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · waves and particles

tracks.announcement_text:
Imagine two small openings through which waves can pass. At a point beyond the openings, the waves may arrive in step, reinforcing one another, or out of step, diminishing one another. A screen can therefore reveal a pattern of bright and dark regions when coherent light passes through two slits.

Quantum experiments with particles can produce analogous patterns of detection. The theory assigns probability amplitudes to the alternatives, and those amplitudes can interfere. Individual detections remain localized, while the distribution built up over many trials reveals the interference.

If the apparatus acquires reliable information distinguishing the two paths, the conditions for interference are altered, and the pattern may be reduced or disappear. The change does not require a conscious creature to stare at the experiment. Physical interactions and the resulting information matter.

The double slit is particularly delightful because a very simple arrangement reveals the inadequacy of merely adding classical probabilities for independent alternatives. The relative phases of the quantum amplitudes can change the result quite dramatically.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the double slit

tracks.announcement_text:
Imagine two notes that can be played separately. A musical arrangement can contain both, with a particular relationship between them. Quantum states admit a mathematical kind of combination called superposition, although the musical comparison has its limits.

A pure quantum state can be expressed as a combination of different basis states, with coefficients called amplitudes. The amplitudes determine probabilities for measurements, and their relative phases influence what happens when the alternatives interfere.

This is not merely a description of our ignorance about a classical object that already has one definite answer in that basis. Two quantum preparations can give the same probabilities for one measurement, yet behave differently in another because their relative phases differ.

When a suitable measurement is performed, it produces an individual recorded result. Questions about how that definite result is related to the preceding quantum description belong to the foundations of the theory.

Superposition is thus not a magical synonym for uncertainty. It is a precise feature of quantum states, with consequences that can be tested in experiments.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · quantum superposition

tracks.announcement_text:
Imagine a very long, regular wave. Its wavelength can be defined quite precisely, but it is difficult to say that the wave occupies one particular small region. To make a localized wave packet, one combines waves with a range of wavelengths. The better localized the packet, the broader that range generally has to be.

Quantum mechanics relates wavelength to momentum. For position and momentum in a given direction, the uncertainty principle places a lower bound on the product of their statistical spreads in a quantum state. A state with an extremely narrow position distribution cannot also have an arbitrarily narrow momentum distribution.

This is more than a limitation of the quality of a measuring instrument. It is a property of the quantum states themselves. Better apparatus can reduce additional measurement errors, but it cannot remove the fundamental relation.

The wave packet offers a useful way of approaching the idea. The two descriptions are related mathematically, and attempting to make one very sharply defined changes what can be said about the other. How elegant, though rather inconvenient for certain classical intuitions.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the uncertainty principle

tracks.announcement_text:
Imagine a ball approaching a hill. If it does not have enough energy to reach the top, classical mechanics says it cannot simply continue over the hill and emerge on the other side.

A quantum particle approaching a finite potential barrier behaves differently. Its quantum state may extend into and beyond the barrier. There can be a nonzero probability of detecting the particle on the far side, even when its energy would not permit passage in the corresponding classical model.

This is quantum tunneling. The probability depends on factors including the barrier's width and height and the properties of the particle. Tunneling has important physical applications, including the operation of scanning tunneling microscopes and certain processes in nuclei.

The particle does not need to borrow extra energy from a secret supply and then return it afterward. The quantum calculation can conserve energy throughout. And the effect is not evidence for an ordinary creature walking through a wall. Our little hill illustrates a difference between classical trajectories and the predictions of a quantum state, not an engineering method for opening a portal.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · quantum tunneling

tracks.announcement_text:
A wave function is a mathematical representation used to describe a pure quantum state. In a simple position representation, the squared magnitude of a normalized wave function gives a probability density. Adding up that density across a region gives the probability of finding the particle there in a position measurement.

The wave function itself contains more information than that probability density alone. Its phase matters when parts of the state are combined. Amplitudes can reinforce or cancel, producing interference that would be lost if we retained only the ordinary probabilities.

When the system is isolated and the appropriate conditions apply, an equation governs the evolution of its quantum state. Together with the measurement rules, that mathematical framework yields extraordinarily successful predictions.

What the wave function ultimately represents is a further question. Some interpretations regard it as describing something physically real; others understand it differently. It is useful to separate the reliable calculation of probabilities from a philosophical claim about the exact nature of the object doing the describing. We can use a remarkably good map while continuing to investigate what its symbols mean.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · what a wave function tells us

tracks.announcement_text:
Quantum mechanics describes states that can evolve as combinations of alternatives. A measuring device, however, leaves a record of a particular outcome: a mark at one location, a number on a display, or a particular result in a detector.

If the device and the system are both described using the same continuous quantum evolution, how should we understand the appearance of that definite recorded result? This is a central part of the measurement problem.

Interactions with the environment can suppress observable interference between alternatives, a process called decoherence. This is an important part of understanding why macroscopic records behave as they do. But different interpretations of quantum mechanics give different accounts of the relation between decoherence, probability, and a particular experienced outcome.

One need not introduce a conscious observer who magically creates the result. There is no established experimental requirement that consciousness perform that task. The question is about the consistency and interpretation of the physical description itself. I rather like the fact that a theory with such impressive predictive success can still leave us with so interesting a question about what its predictions mean.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the measurement problem

tracks.announcement_text:
Schrödinger proposed a rather uncomfortable imaginary experiment involving a cat and a device whose behavior depends on a quantum event. No actual cat is required for our discussion; the thought experiment is about the description of measurement.

Suppose the event has two quantum alternatives, and the device couples them to two very different macroscopic conditions. If we apply the usual continuous quantum evolution to the entire arrangement, the resulting mathematical state can contain both alternatives.

Yet an ordinary observer opening the hypothetical box expects to find one definite condition of the cat. A classical statistical mixture would describe uncertainty about which condition is present, rather than a coherent quantum superposition. How does the quantum description relate to that result?

The purpose of the example is not to establish that ordinary cats spend their days in visibly contradictory conditions. It brings the difficulty of interpreting quantum measurements into a macroscopic setting, where the question is especially striking.

There are different proposed accounts of what happens, and they should not be mistaken for experimentally demonstrated methods of creating such an unfortunate arrangement.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · Schrödinger's cat

tracks.announcement_text:
Two quantum systems can share correlations simply because they were prepared according to the same random instructions. Entanglement is something more. An entangled joint quantum state cannot be explained even as a statistical mixture of separately prepared quantum states for the two systems. The predictions for measurements on the pair depend upon their shared state.

For certain entangled states, measurements made at distant locations exhibit correlations that cannot be reproduced by a simple picture in which each system carries its own predetermined local answers for every possible measurement setting. Experiments have made these correlations particularly interesting.

But an observer cannot choose the random result obtained at one location and thereby transmit a chosen message to the other. The correlations become apparent when the records are compared through ordinary communication. Entanglement does not supply a faster-than-light radio.

This is why I would distinguish the shared description from a mechanism for sending information. The two systems can have a wonderfully nonclassical relationship without giving their observers an unrestricted means of communication. It is a rather important distinction, and one that makes entanglement more interesting than the usual picture of an invisible signal between two particles.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · quantum entanglement

tracks.announcement_text:
Suppose two separated instruments measure particles emitted by a common source. One possible explanation of their results would be that the particles carried predetermined local instructions, with each instrument's result depending only on its local setting and those instructions.

John Bell showed that theories satisfying particular locality and statistical independence assumptions obey restrictions on the correlations they can produce. These restrictions can be expressed as Bell inequalities. Quantum mechanics predicts violations for suitable states and measurements.

Experiments have observed such violations, including experiments designed to close major loopholes. The result rules out the relevant class of local hidden-variable accounts under the assumptions used in the argument. It does not imply that every conceivable hidden-variable theory is impossible.

Nor does violating a Bell inequality allow an experimenter to send a chosen signal faster than light. That is a different property from the observed correlations.

I find Bell's achievement especially delightful because it transformed an apparently philosophical disagreement about the nature of quantum theory into a question that experimentalists could investigate with actual measurements.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · Bell's theorem

tracks.announcement_text:
Quantum teleportation sounds as though it ought to involve a creature disappearing from one room and appearing in another. The real quantum protocol has a different and rather elegant purpose. It transfers the state of a quantum system to another system.

The sender and receiver first share an entangled pair. The sender performs a suitable joint measurement involving the system whose state is to be transferred and the sender's half of the entangled pair. The resulting classical information is communicated to the receiver, who uses it to perform the appropriate correction.

At the end, the receiving system can have the original quantum state. The unknown state has not been copied into two independent versions, and the original material has not been transported through space by the protocol.

The classical message is essential. Until it arrives, the receiver cannot use the arrangement to recover the intended state. Consequently the protocol provides no faster-than-light communication.

The name is wonderfully dramatic, friend, but the actual achievement is sufficiently remarkable without borrowing the properties of a fictional transport spell.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · quantum teleportation

tracks.announcement_text:
Consider a calculation whose alternatives are represented by quantum amplitudes. Unlike ordinary probabilities, amplitudes have phases. When suitable alternatives are combined, their amplitudes can reinforce one another or partially cancel.

A quantum algorithm is a carefully arranged sequence of operations on quantum states. For particular problems, it can exploit interference so that useful outcomes become more likely when the state is measured, while other contributions are suppressed. The relative phases introduced during the calculation can be essential to the result.

It is not enough to prepare a great many alternatives and then demand that a measurement reveal every answer. The measurement yields a particular outcome, and the algorithm must be designed so that the available outcomes convey useful information.

Some quantum algorithms have important theoretical advantages over known classical approaches. For many other problems, no such advantage is established. A quantum computer is therefore not simply a faster version of every conceivable computer. Its interesting abilities arise from a different kind of mathematical arrangement, rather than from the number of alternatives alone.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · interference in quantum computing

tracks.announcement_text:
A classical bit has one of two possible values, conventionally zero and one. A quantum bit, or qubit, has a two-dimensional state space. In a chosen basis, a pure state of the qubit may be expressed as a combination of the zero and one basis states.

Measuring a suitable superposition in that basis can give either outcome, with probabilities determined by the state. But two preparations with the same probabilities in that basis can have different relative phases. A further quantum operation can make those phase differences observable.

That is why a qubit is not merely an ordinary bit about whose value we are uncertain. The mathematical coefficients of its state determine how the alternatives behave when transformed and combined.

There are physical systems that can serve as qubits, including suitable states of atoms, photons and superconducting circuits. They require careful control because unwanted interactions can damage the quantum information being processed. The abstract qubit is a very simple object mathematically; building reliable arrangements of physical qubits is quite another accomplishment.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · qubits

tracks.announcement_text:
One approach to the foundations of quantum mechanics proposes retaining the continuous, unitary evolution of the quantum state without adding a special physical collapse during measurement. This is associated with Hugh Everett and the family of interpretations commonly called many-worlds.

In such accounts, interactions and decoherence can lead to effectively distinct branches of the quantum description. Observers within a branch have records corresponding to particular outcomes. A considerable part of the interpretive work concerns the meaning of those branches and the role of probability.

There are other interpretations of quantum mechanics, including accounts that treat the measurement process differently. The ordinary success of quantum predictions does not, by itself, establish that a particular popular description of branching worlds is the uniquely correct interpretation.

Nor does the mathematical discussion give us a demonstrated way of traveling to an alternative history. I would keep that lovely possibility in its appropriate place among stories and speculative ideas. The genuine foundational question is quite sufficient: what sort of physical reality, if any, should we associate with the full quantum state?
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · many worlds

tracks.announcement_text:
The remarkable feature of a black hole is not simply that its gravity is strong. It possesses a region bounded by an event horizon. From within that region, future-directed light signals cannot reach distant observers outside the black hole.

In general relativity, the geometry of spacetime determines which events can influence which others. The event horizon is a causal boundary, rather than a solid surface that a traveler could strike like the wall of a room.

A black hole does not automatically draw every distant object toward it. At a sufficient distance, an object can orbit a black hole just as it could orbit another concentrated mass. Objects are also not known to pass through black holes into useful alternative destinations. Mathematical extensions and fictional portals are different matters from observed astrophysical objects.

Astronomers have obtained evidence for black holes through their gravitational effects, radiation from surrounding material, and gravitational waves from mergers. Images of their surroundings add another beautiful kind of evidence. We can learn a great deal about an object even when light from within its horizon cannot reach us.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · black holes

tracks.announcement_text:
A sufficiently massive object changes the geometry of spacetime around it. Light passing through that region follows paths determined by the geometry. As a result, a distant source may appear displaced, distorted, magnified, or even represented by several images.

This is gravitational lensing. Imagine a galaxy lying between us and a much more distant source. The arrangement can produce arcs or multiple images around the foreground galaxy. In a particularly symmetric alignment, the image may resemble a ring.

It is not a glass lens suspended between the galaxies. The bending is associated with gravity, and the detailed pattern depends upon the distribution of mass and the relative positions of the source, lens and observer.

Astronomers can use these patterns to investigate mass that would otherwise be difficult to measure, including the distribution of dark matter. I find the method rather delightful. The very distortion that prevents us from seeing a simple, undisturbed image of a distant object becomes a source of information about the intervening universe.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · gravity as a lens

tracks.announcement_text:
When certain distributions of mass change their motion, general relativity predicts disturbances in spacetime that can propagate away from them as gravitational waves. A pair of compact objects orbiting and eventually merging can produce a particularly strong signal.

As a gravitational wave passes, it changes the relative separations of freely falling objects in a characteristic way. Instruments such as those used by the LIGO observatories compare the travel of light along long perpendicular arms to detect extraordinarily small changes in distance.

The first direct detection was made in twenty fifteen, from the merger of two black holes. It provided a new means of observing events that need not announce themselves through ordinary visible light.

You may have heard the little chirp associated with such a signal. That is an audible representation of the measured waveform, not sound waves from the black holes traveling through the vacuum of space. The distinction is a lovely example of the difference between a physical signal and the form in which we choose to present it to our senses.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · gravitational waves

tracks.announcement_text:
When astronomers examine the motions of stars in galaxies, the movements of galaxies within clusters, and the way gravity bends distant light, they find patterns that are difficult to account for using the observed ordinary matter alone under the usual gravitational framework.

Dark matter is the name given to a component of the standard cosmological account that helps explain those gravitational observations. It does not emit or absorb light in the ordinary ways that would make it directly visible to telescopes. Its presence is inferred from its effects and from several independent lines of cosmological evidence.

The identity of that component remains uncertain. Researchers investigate possible particles and other proposals, and some explore whether modifications to gravity can account for parts of the evidence. A convincing alternative must explain the wider collection of observations, not merely one interesting curve.

The name is not an explanation of its microscopic nature. Nor does it refer to the dark energy associated with accelerated cosmic expansion. We have substantial evidence for an unanswered physical question, which is quite a different thing from having no evidence at all.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · dark matter

tracks.announcement_text:
Observations of the distant universe indicate that the expansion of the universe is accelerating in the standard cosmological description. That is rather surprising if one begins by considering only the gravitational attraction of ordinary matter.

The term dark energy refers to whatever accounts for the accelerated expansion within that description. A cosmological constant, which can be represented as a constant energy density associated with space, is one important model. Other theoretical accounts are also investigated.

It is not the same thing as dark matter. Dark matter helps explain gravitational clustering and the motions and lensing patterns of galaxies. Dark energy is associated with the large-scale expansion history. The two names refer to different problems, even though both remain incompletely understood.

And dark energy is not a supply of mysterious fuel whose practical use has already been established. We use the term because it identifies a contribution needed in a successful model of the observations. The next question is what, physically, that contribution represents. A very large question for a very small name.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · dark energy

tracks.announcement_text:
A light-year is a unit of distance, not a duration. It is the distance that light travels in a vacuum during one year. The name is useful because the distances between stars are so great that ordinary kilometers become rather cumbersome numbers.

If a star is one hundred light-years away, in a simple setting where the distance and motion can be treated in the usual way, the light reaching us from it has spent about one hundred years traveling. We see the star as it was when that light was emitted, not as it might be described at this instant in some chosen distant reference frame.

For very distant galaxies in an expanding universe, the relation between distance and light travel time requires more careful definitions. The basic observation remains: receiving light gives us information about past events.

Looking into the sky is therefore a remarkable way of examining history. But the telescope has not carried its observer bodily into the past. It has received a signal that has been traveling through space since an earlier event.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · light-years and old light

tracks.announcement_text:
Quantum theory, in its usual description of an isolated system, evolves states in a way that preserves the information needed in principle to reverse that evolution. General relativity predicts black holes with event horizons, and a semiclassical calculation by Stephen Hawking suggests that black holes can emit radiation and gradually lose mass.

The difficulty arises if a black hole evaporates completely and its radiation appears to retain no adequate record of the original quantum information. How can such a process agree with quantum theory's information-preserving evolution?

That is the black hole information paradox. It concerns quantum information and the consistency of fundamental theories, not merely the practical difficulty of recovering a lost book from beyond a horizon.

There has been substantial theoretical progress, including calculations suggesting ways in which information may be encoded in the radiation. But a complete experimentally established account of the quantum physics of realistic evaporating black holes remains unavailable.

I find this problem particularly interesting because it brings two extraordinarily successful descriptions of nature into contact precisely where their compatibility is most difficult to establish.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the black hole information paradox

tracks.announcement_text:
A familiar optical hologram contains information on a surface that allows a three-dimensional-looking image to be reconstructed. The holographic principle in theoretical physics takes its name from a rather different, mathematical idea.

The entropy associated with a black hole is proportional to the area of its horizon, rather than simply to the volume enclosed by it. This surprising result helped motivate proposals in which information describing a region of spacetime can be related to degrees of freedom on a lower-dimensional boundary.

In certain theoretical models, there are particularly striking mathematical correspondences between a theory involving gravity in a higher-dimensional space and a different theory defined on its boundary. These are important tools in research on quantum gravity.

This is not an experimental discovery that ordinary reality is a projected video, nor an assertion that a creature could peel away a hidden screen behind the stars. The word holographic expresses an analogy about the organization of information. The actual mathematical relationships are more precise, and their application to our universe remains a subject of research.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the holographic principle

tracks.announcement_text:
Imagine an extraordinary hotel with rooms numbered one, two, three, and so on without end. Every room is occupied. A new guest arrives. Can the hotel accommodate that guest without sending any of the existing guests away?

The proprietor asks each guest to move from their present room to the next numbered room. The guest in room one goes to room two; the guest in room two goes to room three; and the same rule applies to every room. No two existing guests have been assigned the same new room, and room one is now available.

A finite hotel cannot solve its lack of room in that fashion. The final guest would have nowhere to go. In the imagined infinite hotel, however, there is no final numbered room.

Hilbert's hotel illustrates a property of countably infinite sets. The positive integers can be placed into a one-to-one correspondence with the integers beginning at two, even though the latter collection is a proper subset of the former. Infinity does not obey all the intuitions we acquire from counting finite collections.

A most curious establishment. I suspect its proprietor would have rather a lot of paperwork.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · Hilbert's hotel

tracks.announcement_text:
There are infinitely many positive integers, and also infinitely many integers when we include zero and the negative ones. Yet we can arrange all the integers in a sequence: zero, one, negative one, two, negative two, and so on. Each receives a position in a list indexed by the positive integers.

These sets are called countably infinite. But not every infinite set can be listed that way. Georg Cantor's diagonal argument shows that a proposed list of all real numbers between zero and one must omit some real number. One can construct a decimal expansion differing from the first listed number in its first digit, the second in its second digit, and so forth, with a suitable choice of digits to avoid ambiguous representations.

The constructed number cannot equal any entry on the list. No matter how the list was arranged, something would remain outside it.

Thus the real numbers form an uncountable set, and their cardinality is larger than that of the positive integers. How delightful that we can make a precise distinction between different infinities without having to finish counting either one.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · different sizes of infinity

tracks.announcement_text:
Suppose two mathematical descriptions begin with values that differ by an exceedingly small amount. Both evolve according to exactly the same deterministic rules. One might expect their subsequent behavior to remain nearly identical.

In some nonlinear dynamical systems, a small initial difference can grow substantially as the systems evolve. This sensitivity is an important feature of deterministic chaos. The rules do not need to contain a random choice for a long-term prediction to become very difficult.

Weather provides a familiar setting in which such limitations matter. Measurements of the initial state are never infinitely precise, and small uncertainties can grow. This does not mean that a particular butterfly has been established as the cause of a particular storm. That famous image illustrates sensitivity, not a simple chain of blame.

There is a distinction between determinism and predictability. A system may have definite mathematical rules and still resist accurate long-range prediction when its starting state is known only approximately. A rather useful distinction for anypony who has ever attempted to contemplate the weather.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · deterministic chaos

tracks.announcement_text:
The universe contains an extraordinary number of stars, many with planets. Suppose that technological civilizations develop relatively often, that some persist for a long time, and that some produce signals or structures we could detect. Why, then, have we not obtained compelling evidence of such a civilization beyond Earth?

This family of questions is often called the Fermi paradox. Its force depends upon the assumptions one makes. We do not yet know how frequently life begins, how often it develops technological capabilities, how long detectable activity persists, or which kinds of evidence a distant civilization might produce.

The distances and times involved are immense. Our searches cover only parts of the enormous space of possible locations, frequencies, signal types and observing times. A lack of detections is not the same as a comprehensive census of all civilizations.

There are many proposed answers, but no established conclusion. I find that restraint rather important. The question is an invitation to improve our observations and examine our assumptions, not a proof that we are alone or that somebody must already be hiding nearby.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · the Fermi question

tracks.announcement_text:
A common image of a wormhole is a sheet of paper folded so that two distant points lie close together, with a short passage connecting them. The image is helpful for imagining a shortcut, but a physical wormhole would involve the geometry of spacetime, not a literal sheet folded in an ordinary room.

Certain mathematical spacetime models contain wormhole-like connections. Whether such a connection could be traversed, maintained, or formed under physically realistic conditions is a separate and difficult question. Traversable models generally require unusual conditions on the matter or energy supporting their geometry.

Some theoretical arrangements have also been considered in discussions of time travel and closed timelike curves. That does not make an astrophysical black hole a demonstrated wormhole, or provide evidence that a usable time machine has been constructed.

I enjoy the geometry very much, friend. But I would distinguish a mathematically interesting spacetime, a physically possible configuration, and a demonstrated means of transportation. There is a considerable distance between those three accomplishments. It may take rather more than a fold in a piece of paper to cross it.
tracks.title: science in a pocket dimension · wormholes and time machines

tracks.announcement_text: there is an entire chapter on crow omens in the sixth-century Sanskrit work known as the Bṛhat Saṃhitā. it attends to the direction of the bird, the season, even the tree in which it nests. the meaning of a direction can change with the region. i thought of Pinkie Pie, friend, and the little dictionary of signs she carries in her own body. a twitching tail foretells something falling, while flapping ears mean something else entirely. poor Twilight had quite an afternoon learning the difference.
tracks.title: arcana: the cries of crows

tracks.announcement_text: in the early Japanese chronicles, a sacred crow named Yatagarasu is sent to guide the future Emperor Jimmu from Kumano toward Yamato. the familiar images of the crow have three legs, though the early chronicles do not actually specify them. i like a story in which a bird knows the way. when Spike ran away from Ponyville, it was Owlowiscious who discovered his little ketchup-covered footprints. Twilight followed them all the way to the dragon’s cave, and the owl helped bring them both out of the dark.
tracks.title: arcana: a bird to show the way

tracks.announcement_text: some medieval European books of medicine preserve prayers and magical charms alongside remedies. a single manuscript could contain several approaches to healing, and its particular history tells us something about the people who used it. i remember Fluttershy at her books, discovering that the healer called the Mystical Mask was Mage Meadowbrook. later, she noticed that Meadowbrook’s mask bore stripes like the queen of the flash bees. there was the missing clue to how the old healer had obtained the honey for her cure.
tracks.title: arcana: the healer’s manuscript
